messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 57
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Physical Therapist
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 39

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Somatic (Nausea): Feeling nauseous, Name Reminders: Hearing related names, Visual (Water/Flooding): Water, flooding, or large bodies of water
  Maladaptive Strategies: Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out, Past Dwelling: I dwell on how I used to be before the event, Avoid Going Out: Going out
  Threat: Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
  Memory: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Vignette:
Marisol Vega is a 57-year-old divorced Latina woman who has worked as a physical therapist for nearly three decades, most recently at an outpatient rehabilitation clinic in the Gulf Coast region of Texas. She presents for an initial psychological evaluation approximately fourteen months after surviving a major hurricane that struck her coastal community, reporting a constellation of distressing symptoms that have progressively narrowed the boundaries of her daily life.

The storm made landfall on a Tuesday morning in late August. Marisol had chosen not to evacuate, having ridden out lesser storms before and feeling a responsibility to her elderly neighbor, Dolores, who lived alone next door. What she had not anticipated was the speed of the surge. Within two hours of the storm's landfall, the water was at her windowsills. She remembers standing on her kitchen counter, watching the brown water rise around her furniture, holding Dolores's hand as the older woman wept. The surge eventually stabilized just below ceiling height in her ground floor, and the two women spent eleven hours in the attic before rescue teams reached them by boat. Dolores survived, but a family two streets over did not, and Marisol learned this only when she returned to survey the damage weeks later. She had watched the water from her attic window for hours — that particular quality of light on moving, opaque floodwater, the debris turning slowly in it — and that image has never fully left her.

In the weeks that followed, Marisol noticed that something had shifted in the way she held the memory of those hours. Rather than recalling it as something that had happened to her, she found herself relating to it the way one might relate to a story heard about a stranger. The memory feels like it belongs to someone else, she told her evaluator quietly, and yet the grief it carries does not. There are moments — triggered by nothing she can name, or by a sound, or by a sudden wave of nausea — when the full emotional weight of those eleven hours descends on her without any accompanying image. She simply finds herself grieving, intensely and without context, in the middle of a treatment session or while eating breakfast.

Water, in any form, has become difficult. Marisol drives a longer route to work to avoid a particular overpass above a retention pond. At the clinic, she has quietly rearranged her schedule to avoid the hydrotherapy pool, telling colleagues she prefers land-based techniques, which is true now in a way it was not before. When a patient's name is Dolores, or when someone mentions a place name associated with the storm — even tangentially, in passing conversation — she feels a jolt of nausea and has learned to excuse herself briefly. The nausea itself, arriving without warning, has become its own source of dread. She had come to believe that her body was no longer trustworthy, that it carried information her mind refused to organize.

Her sleep has been poor since the storm. She lies awake listening to the sounds of the neighborhood, and any sudden noise — a car backfiring, a door slamming somewhere down the hall — brings her fully upright, heart pounding. She feels safe, she said, only in two places: her bedroom with the door closed, and her office at the clinic with the blinds drawn. Everywhere else requires a vigilance that exhausts her. She has largely stopped going out socially. A divorce finalized three years before the storm had already reduced her social world, and the hurricane has contracted it further. Friends have stopped calling as often. She knows this and dwells on it — on who she was before, the woman who hosted dinner parties, who kayaked on weekends, who was known among her patients for her steadiness and warmth. She spends considerable time in that comparison, and the distance between that woman and her present self feels, on difficult days, unbridgeable.

What finally brought Marisol to seek help was a session last month in which she was guiding a patient through gait exercises near the clinic's exterior windows during a rainstorm. She found herself unable to continue and had to ask a colleague to cover. She had never before been unable to do her job. What she most hopes for, she said, is to be able to stand near a window in the rain and simply be a physical therapist again.
